definitions.definition: Ω=ℝ^n × (0,∞), the domain of u, with the relative Euclidean smooth structure.

definitions.type: partial differentiation notation on the open domain Ω
definitions.definition: ∂ denotes ordinary coordinate partial differentiation, component by component for vector-valued functions. Subscripts t and tt denote one and two time derivatives, x_j and x_jx_j denote one and two derivatives in spatial coordinate j, and x_jt denotes first time then spatial differentiation. Thus u_t=∂_t u, u_tt=∂_t∂_t u and ∂_{x_j}u_t=∂_{x_j}∂_t u. The same notation applies to any differentiable real scalar function. Derivatives are used only where their existence has been established. For native total-function source applications, a function on Ω may be extended by zero outside Ω; at points of Ω all derivatives refer to its germ on Ω, independent of the extension.

definitions.type: spatial Laplacian on vector-valued twice differentiable functions on Ω

definitions.definition: e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|²+Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|². All norms are Euclidean; the spatial sum is the Frobenius square of the spatial gradient.

E(t)=∫_{ℝ^n}e(x,t) dx for t>0. For definiteness this is the total real Bochner integral convention (zero if not integrable); the proof separately proves integrability for every t>0, so the intended ordinary finite Lebesgue integral is obtained.

definitions.type: Lebesgue measure and integration notation on finite real coordinate spaces
definitions.definition: dx is standard Lebesgue measure on ℝ^n, identified with the finite product of one-dimensional Lebesgue measures in standard coordinates. On other real coordinate spaces the same notation means their standard Lebesgue measure, including mass one on the zero-dimensional space. Integrable means measurable with finite integral of the absolute value. A set indicator 1_A is 1 on A and 0 elsewhere, for any set A in the integration space.
v·w=dot(v,w)=Σ_{k=1}^d v_k w_k for v,w∈ℝ^d and any finite dimension d; |v|²=v·v.

inputs.statement: u is jointly smooth on ℝ^n × (0,∞).

All positive-order partial derivatives of u are smooth on Ω; e and e_t are continuous there. For every (x,t)∈Ω, u·u_t=0 and u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu)=0, and e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2Σ_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t. Mixed time and spatial second derivatives agree. At each such point, every scalar a satisfying u_tt−Δ_xu=a u equals Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|².

For every t0>0, put J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. There exist a compact C⊂ℝ^n and real R>0 such that C⊂(−R,R)^n, u(x,r)=q whenever x∉C and r∈J, and Q=[−R,R]^n is compact and measurable with finite Lebesgue measure (2R)^n. On (ℝ^n\C)×int J every positive-order derivative of u is zero. For every r∈int J, the following spatial scalar functions are continuous, vanish outside C, have compact support contained in C, are bounded on Q, and are Lebesgue integrable: e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t·u_tt, u_t·Δ_xu, and, for every j=1,...,n, ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, g_j=u_t·∂_{x_j}u and ∂_{x_j}g_j. The functions g_j are smooth in space. For each of these scalar functions its absolute integral is at most some finite nonnegative bound on its absolute value on Q times (2R)^n. For every real b, the function b 1_Q is integrable on ℝ^n. In particular e(·,t) is integrable for every t>0.

inputs.statement: For every t>0, E is differentiable at t and E'(t)=∫_{ℝ^n}e_t(x,t)dx = 2∫_{ℝ^n}u_t(x,t)·u_tt(x,t)dx +2Σ_{j=1}^n∫_{ℝ^n}∂_{x_j}u(x,t)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t)dx. Every integral displayed is finite.
For every t>0 and j∈{1,...,n}, ∫_{ℝ^n} ∂_{x_j}u(x,t)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t)dx = −∫_{ℝ^n}u_t(x,t)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t)dx. Both integrals are finite.

For a normed additive commutative group V and real normed space V, f:ℝ→V and real a,b,C, if f is differentiable on [a,b] and |derivWithin(f,[a,b],r)|≤C for every r∈[a,b), then for every z∈[a,b], |f(z)−f(a)|≤C(z−a).

Its derivative within [a,b] has norm at most C on [a,b).

output.statement: For every real t>0, e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on ℝ^n, E is differentiable at t, and E'(t)=0. Moreover E(s)=E(t) for all real s,t>0. The energy is exactly ∫_{ℝ^n} (|u_t|²+Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|²) dx, without a factor 1/2; no conclusion at time zero is asserted.

locals.declaration: Fix an arbitrary positive real s.
Fix an arbitrary positive real t and consider the three possible orders of the endpoints.

argument.text: For every t>0, N002 gives integrability of e(·,t). N003 proves differentiability of E there and its derivative formula. For each such t substitute N004 into that formula and use linearity for the finite integrable sum, obtaining E'(t)=2∫u_t·u_tt dx−2Σ_j∫u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx=2∫u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu) dx. N001 makes the last integrand identically zero. Thus E'(t)=0 for every t>0. H002 supplies the smoothness guard on the definitions of e and E.

produces.statement: For every real t>0, e(·,t) is integrable, E is differentiable at t and E'(t)=0.

argument.text: For arbitrary positive real endpoints s<t, F001 gives differentiability throughout [s,t] and zero derivative there. M004 with real function E and C=0 gives |E(t)−E(s)|≤0, and therefore equality. If the endpoints coincide equality is immediate, and if their order is reversed exchange them. This proves E(s)=E(t) for all s,t>0. In invoking the native total-function M004, extend E by zero at nonpositive times; [s,t] is inside its positive domain so this does not affect any derivative. The defining energy retains coefficient 1 on both squares and there is no assertion at time zero. Together with F001 this is exactly P.

applications.bindings: V=ℝ,f=E extended by zero for nonpositive arguments,a=s,b=t,z=t,C=0, for arbitrary 0<s<t.

F001 gives differentiability on a neighborhood of [s,t]⊂(0,∞).
F001 gives ordinary derivative zero. On the nondegenerate interval the within derivative agrees with it, hence has norm at most zero on [s,t).
